memory_update.text: AXTI should be tracked as the cleanest underfollowed US-listed compound-substrate candidate for AI optical networking, but survival to later layers requires customer qualification and data-center revenue evidence.
COHR and LITE are reference leaders rather than discovery names; they help validate demand and identify bottlenecks upstream in InP substrates, laser chips, and optical-component manufacturing.

POET is a speculative shadow candidate near CPO and optical-engine integration; it should not be treated as a substrate chokepoint without evidence of production-scale adoption and material supplier dependence.

Next Layer 1C/2 work should search for non-US or OTC-listed substrate suppliers, private substrate vendors, and named supplier relationships for Lumentum, Coherent, POET, Fabrinet, Innolight, and other 800G/1.6T module makers.

AXTI should remain the primary underfollowed direct-substrate candidate for this node because SEC filings explicitly connect InP substrates to hyperscale, AI, silicon-photonics and PIC applications and describe a very small primary-supplier base.

VECO should be tracked as an upstream equipment/capacity-constraint candidate for InP laser manufacturing rather than as a substrate supplier; evidence focus should be order quality, customer identity, backlog conversion and exposure size.

LITE and COHR validate demand pull into InP-based optical components for 800G/1.6T and CPO, but they are less pure for the substrate chokepoint and should mainly serve as reference or near-reference anchors.

Layer 2 should verify market caps, analyst coverage, 2025-2026 segment revenue, customer concentration, China/export-control risk, and whether InP/GaAs substrate tightness is independently confirmed by primary filings or customer qualification disclosures.

AXTI should be promoted to the next verification layer as the closest US-listed direct compound-substrate candidate for InP/GaAs/Ge exposure tied to optical communications and data-center connectivity.
MTRN remains a plausible but weakly proven precision-materials candidate; survival depends on finding direct optical-transceiver, silicon-photonics, laser, or CPO customer evidence.
COHR defines the reference stack: InP wafers, lasers, modulators, photodiodes, 1.6T transceiver components, and CPO laser sources. Smaller candidates should be tested against this stack.
The biggest evidence gap is not whether AI optical demand exists, but whether independent small/mid-cap material suppliers have qualified supply positions at 800G/1.6T transceiver or CPO customers.
AXTI should be promoted to the next research layer as the cleanest US-listed underfollowed direct substrate candidate for InP/GaAs exposure tied to AI optical networking.

COHR and LITE are not pure substrate suppliers but are important demand and chokepoint validators because their InP lasers, photonic devices, transceivers, and AI datacenter optical components sit immediately above the substrate layer.
MTRN remains a speculative shadow candidate until direct exposure to optical transceiver, InP/GaAs, silicon photonics, optical coating, or CPO supply chains is proven from primary disclosures.

Key verification gap: quantify which US-listed companies have merchant InP substrate revenue versus internal InP device/module revenue, and identify whether hyperscaler AI demand is direct, through transceiver customers, or merely inferred from the broader optical cycle.

Adjacent picks-and-shovels exposure appears in VECO, which sells MOCVD, wet-processing and ion-beam tools for InP laser manufacturing. LITE and COHR are included as higher-attention reference/near-reference optical-component leaders because their InP laser, 800G/1.6T and CPO exposure helps validate demand pull through the substrate and epiwafer chain.
